name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Thursday 8 June 1972

clue.text: Cider from the wood — bill not from this

definitions.text: Cider from the wood — bill not from this

blocks.note: surface reading: draught cider poured straight from the cask
setter's reading: a growth on a tree that sounds like a cider fruit, yet nobody could brew or sell a drink from it

explanation.surface: A drinker orders cask cider and grumbles about the bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From the wood' means from the barrel in a pub, but here it means growing on a tree; the 'apple' on an oak is a gall, so no cider and no bill.
explanation.definitionFit: An oak-apple is a round gall caused by wasp larvae on oak twigs, an apple in name only.

clue.text: Posture of a striker, perhaps?

blocks.note: surface reading: the stance a batsman or footballer takes
setter's reading: a worker on strike adopts a defiant stance, a word for both physical posture and a mindset

explanation.surface: How a sportsman stands when about to hit the ball.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means both a bodily posture and a combative frame of mind, which a picketing striker certainly has.
explanation.definitionFit: Attitude is a bodily position or stance and also a defiant, uncooperative manner.

clue.text: It's a secondary consideration

blocks.note: surface reading: something of lesser importance
setter's reading: an idea that occurs second in time, coming later than the first

explanation.walkthrough: 'Secondary' reads as minor in importance, but it is meant as coming second in time.
explanation.definitionFit: Something thought of later, added once the main plan has already been made.

clue.text: "I have Liken all know ledge to be my " (Bacon)

definitions.text: "I have Liken all know ledge to be my " (Bacon)

blocks.clueFragment: "I have Liken all know ledge to be my "
blocks.note: a quotation with its last word left blank
Francis Bacon wrote in a 1592 letter to Lord Burghley that he had taken all knowledge to be his own territory

explanation.walkthrough: The printed text is garbled: it should read 'I have taken all knowledge to be my ...'. The missing word completes Bacon's famous claim.
explanation.definitionFit: A province is a sphere of activity or field of expertise, here the whole of learning.

clue.text: A girl has no real following in Worcestershire

definitions.note: a place in Worcestershire; the definition names where the answer is

blocks.note: Eve, a girl's name
a sham is not real; placed after the girl

explanation.surface: A young woman has a fake fan club somewhere in the English Midlands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' tells you the second piece comes after the first. Worcestershire is an English county in the West Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Evesham is a market town on the River Avon in Worcestershire, famous for its fruit-growing vale.

clue.text: Resting-place for flood survivors

blocks.note: surface reading: an emergency shelter after a modern flood
setter's reading: the Flood of Genesis, whose survivors were Noah's family and animals in the ark

explanation.walkthrough: Genesis says the ark came to rest on the mountains of this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Mount Ararat in Turkey is traditionally where Noah's ark grounded when the waters fell.

clue.text: Soldiers get no synchronization out of it

definitions.text: Soldiers get no synchronization out of it

blocks.note: surface reading: troops failing to coordinate
setter's reading: soldiers who are 'out of' this thing are marching unevenly

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom is 'out of step': marching soldiers whose feet do not land together.
explanation.definitionFit: Marching in step means moving feet in unison, so being out of it destroys synchronised marching.

clue.text: A prude's self-description is at the beginning

blocks.note: a prude would say of themselves 'I'm prim'
taken as written

explanation.surface: A prudish person describes themselves at the start of a conversation.
explanation.definitionFit: Imprimis is a Latin adverb meaning in the first place, used to open a list.

clue.text: Word for word — an uncommonly brave boy

indicators.note: uncommonly means in an unusual way, so the following word is set out in an unusual order

blocks.note: the letters of brave rearranged
Tim, a boy's name

explanation.surface: A literal account of a remarkably courageous young lad.
explanation.definitionFit: Verbatim describes repeating something in exactly the same words as originally spoken.

clue.text: Steer the children back

indicators.note: back tells you to read the word for the children in the opposite direction

blocks.note: tots are small children

explanation.walkthrough: 'Steer' looks like a verb, but it is the noun: a young castrated bull. Stot is a Scottish and northern English dialect word for one.
explanation.definitionFit: A stot is a bullock, a young castrated ox, which is exactly what a steer is.

clue.text: He listens-in without a licence

blocks.note: surface reading: someone tuning a radio without paying for the UK broadcast receiving licence
setter's reading: someone overhearing a private conversation without permission

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain and Australia, radio sets once needed a paid licence; 'listening-in' was the period term for hearing the wireless.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who secretly overhears other people's private talk, originally by standing under the eaves of a house.

clue.text: I hear prisons might hold churchgoers

indicators.note: might suggests a possible rearrangement of the words before it rather than their given order

blocks.note: all twelve letters used

explanation.surface: Someone has heard that jails may be housing members of a congregation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I hear' looks like a homophone signal, but here it is simply part of the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Parishioners are members of a parish who attend its church services.

clue.text: He narrowly misses being a 17

blocks.note: surface reading: a person who just fails to be an outsider, someone on the fringes
setter's reading: a fastener sewn on the outside of a coat, it is nearly but not quite an outsider since it passes through to the inside

explanation.walkthrough: 17 refers to the answer at 17-down, OUTSIDER. A button sits on the outer face of a garment, so it is very nearly one.
explanation.definitionFit: A button is a small disc sewn onto clothing to fasten it, sitting just on the outer surface.

clue.text: A bit of a mess, needing more NATO manoeuvre

indicators.note: a manoeuvre moves troops into new positions, so these letters are moved around

blocks.note: all eight letters used

explanation.surface: A disorderly military situation calls for another NATO exercise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mess' suggests disorder, but it is an officers' mess, the dining and social quarters; an anteroom is one of its rooms.
explanation.definitionFit: An anteroom is a lounge or sitting room within a military officers' mess, so it is part of one.

clue.text: He's keen to make his mark in the river

indicators.note: in places the word for making one's mark inside the name of the river

blocks.note: the Dee, a river in Wales, England and Scotland
a voter makes his mark, a cross on the ballot paper

explanation.surface: An eager man wants to make his name on the river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dee is a river name crosswords use constantly; voting is 'making your mark' because ballots are marked with a cross.
explanation.definitionFit: A devotee is an enthusiast, someone ardently attached to a cause or pursuit.

clue.text: Politician expresses vexation about a come-back

indicators.note: back tells you to read the following word in the opposite direction
about means surrounding, so the exclamation goes around the other piece

blocks.note: drat is an exclamation of vexation
taken as written

explanation.surface: A politician voices annoyance about having to stage a comeback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come-back' looks like one word, but its parts split: the word come, then the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A Democrat is a politician of the US Democratic Party, or any advocate of democracy.

clue.text: Costers might find the change bracing

definitions.note: the clue uses an adjective for things that brace; the answer is a plural noun

indicators.note: a change alters the order of the letters in the word before it

blocks.note: costers are costermongers, London street sellers of fruit and vegetables

explanation.surface: Street traders might find a change of scene invigorating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bracing' suggests a refreshing breeze, but the answer is close-fitting undergarments that brace the body.
explanation.definitionFit: Corsets are stiff fitted undergarments that support and shape the torso, literally bracing it.

clue.text: He doesn't get a look-in; but who else could?

definitions.text: He doesn't get a look-in; but who else could?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone with no chance, a rank long shot
setter's reading: only a person standing outside a window could literally look in

explanation.walkthrough: 'Get a look-in' is an idiom for having a chance; taken literally, looking in is something done from outside.
explanation.definitionFit: An outsider is a competitor thought unlikely to win, and also someone not part of the group.

clue.text: It compelled people to pay their way

definitions.text: It compelled people to pay their way

blocks.clueFragment: compelled people to pay their way
blocks.note: surface reading: something forcing people to be financially independent
setter's reading: paying literally to use a road

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pay one's way' means to cover one's own costs; here it is paying for the way, the road itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrier across a turnpike road where travellers had to hand over a fee before passing.

clue.text: Difficulties for the navigator

blocks.note: first meaning: hardship
second meaning: narrow sea channels a navigator must steer through

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is loose: these are things a navigator deals with.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a state of trouble and narrow waterways connecting two seas.

clue.text: Basingstoke abated her Gilbertian madness

blocks.note: surface reading: a Hampshire town that somehow cured someone's madness
setter's reading: in Gilbert and Sullivan's Ruddigore, the word Basingstoke is the code word that calms a mad heroine

explanation.walkthrough: In Ruddigore, Mad Margaret's husband says 'Basingstoke' whenever her madness returns, and she instantly recovers.
explanation.definitionFit: Mad Margaret is the deranged character in the comic opera Ruddigore by W. S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan.

clue.text: Just the thing for junketing

blocks.note: surface reading: going on a jaunt or feast, often at public expense
setter's reading: the ingredient needed to make junket, a sweet set-milk dessert

explanation.walkthrough: Junketing usually means partying on someone else's money, but junket is also a milk pudding.
explanation.definitionFit: Rennet is the enzyme preparation that curdles milk, used to set junket and to make cheese.

clue.text: Not much to cat

blocks.note: first meaning: a small amount
second meaning: a pudding to eat; the printed 'cat' is a misprint for 'eat'

explanation.walkthrough: The clue should read 'Not much to eat'. A trifle is a layered British dessert of sponge, fruit, custard and cream.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a small trivial amount and also a cold layered pudding served for dessert.

clue.text: One example of those goings-on

blocks.note: surface reading: some scandalous or suspicious activity
setter's reading: a single instance of going on, that is, carrying on further

explanation.walkthrough: 'Goings-on' suggests misbehaviour, but read literally it is the act of going on.
explanation.definitionFit: A continuation is the act of carrying on or extending something without stopping.

clue.text: Green missing? Then it's all off

definitions.text: Green missing? Then it's all off

blocks.note: surface reading: a lost village green or golf green
setter's reading: without the green traffic light, the signal to proceed is absent

explanation.walkthrough: Green is the traffic-light colour meaning go, so with no green there is no permission to proceed.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-go is a situation that is impossible or cancelled, as when permission is refused.

clue.text: He was done out of his rights by a smooth character

definitions.text: He was done out of his rights by a smooth character

blocks.clueFragment: done out of his rights by a smooth character
blocks.note: surface reading: someone swindled by a slick con man
setter's reading: Jacob, the smooth-skinned brother in Genesis who took his hairy twin's birthright and blessing

explanation.walkthrough: Genesis 27 has Jacob say 'my brother is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man'.
explanation.definitionFit: Esau, elder son of Isaac, sold his birthright to Jacob and was later tricked out of his father's blessing.

clue.text: "Rightly to be great is not to stir without great " (Hamlet)

definitions.text: "Rightly to be great is not to stir without great " (Hamlet)

blocks.clueFragment: "Rightly to be great is not to stir without great "
blocks.note: a quotation with its last word left blank
from Hamlet's soliloquy in Act 4, Scene 4, on Fortinbras marching to war over a trifle

explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet reflects that true greatness does not act without a great cause, yet will fight over a straw when honour is at stake.
explanation.definitionFit: Argument here has the older sense of a subject or cause for action, a reason to act.

clue.text: Underlines the direction to the locks

blocks.note: S for south, a compass direction
tresses are locks of hair

explanation.surface: Someone emphasises the way to the canal locks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Locks' suggests canals or doors, but it means hair.
explanation.definitionFit: To stress something is to emphasise it, just as underlining a word does.
